CLAY HUMERICKHOUSE,

vs.

STATE OF ILLINOIS/MURPHYSBORO LIFE 
SKILLS RE-ENTRY CENTER, 
 
 
Respondent. 
 
 
 
DECISION AND OPINION ON REVIEW 
 
 
Timely Petition for Review having been filed by the Respondent herein and notice given 
to all parties, the Commission, after considering the issues of accident, causal connection, medical 
expenses, prospective medical, temporary total disability, and permanent partial disability and 
being advised of the facts and law, affirms and adopts the Decision of the Arbitrator, which is 
attached hereto and made a part hereof.   
 
 
The Commission agrees with the Arbitrator’s award of temporary total disability benefits 
but disagrees with the calculation of weeks and parts thereof, finding the total period of disability 
equates to 6 1/7 weeks.  Therefore, the Commission modifies the third paragraph of the Order of 
the Arbitration Decision, striking, “6 weeks” and replacing it with, “6 1/7 weeks.”   
 
 
The Commission further modifies the award of medical, striking the first and second 
paragraphs of the Order, and replacing it with, “Petitioner is awarded reasonable, necessary, and 
related medical pursuant to Section 8(a) and 8.2 of the Act, as outlined in PX1.  Respondent shall 
receive credit for any bills paid by its group medical plan pursuant to Section 8(j).  Respondent 
shall hold Petitioner harmless for any bills for which they are claiming said credit”.  Additionally, 
the last paragraph of Issue (J) on page 9 of the Decision shall be stricken and replaced with, 
“Respondent is therefore ordered to pay reasonable, necessary, and related medical pursuant to 
§8(a) and 8.2 of the Act, as outlined in PX1.  Respondent shall receive credit for any bills paid by

24 WC 12632 
Page 2 
 
its group medical plan pursuant to §8(j).  Respondent shall hold Petitioner harmless for any bills 
for which they are claiming said credit”. 
 
The Commission further modifies the first paragraph under Issue (J) on page 9 of the 
Decision, striking, “Upon establishing causal connection and the reasonableness and the necessity 
of recommended medical treatment, employers are responsible for necessary prospective medical 
care required by their employees. Plantation Mfg. Co. v. Indus. Comm’n, 294 Ill.App.3d 705, 691 
N.E.2d. 13 (1997). This includes treatment required to diagnose, relieve, or cure the effects of 
claimant's injury. F & B Mfg. Co. v. Indus. Comm'n, 325 Ill. App. 3d 527, 758 N.E.2d 18 (2001)” 
and replacing it with, “Under section 8(a) of the Act, the claimant is entitled to recover reasonable 
medical expenses that are causally related to the accident and that are determined to be required to 
diagnose, relieve, or cure the effects of claimant's injury. F & B Mfg. Co. v. Indus. Comm'n, 325 
Ill. App. 3d 527 (2001), citing, University of Illinois v. Indus. Comm'n, 232 Ill. App. 3d 154, 164 
(1992).” 
 
Finally, the Commission further modifies factor (v) of the §8.1b analysis under Issue (L) 
on page 10 of the Decision, adding at the end of the paragraph, “The Arbitrator assigns significant 
weight to this factor.”  
 
 
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that the Decision of the 
Arbitrator filed July 31, 2025 is hereby affirmed and adopted. 
 
 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that Respondent shall pay 
Petitioner temporary total disability benefits in the amount of $834.64/week for 6 1/7 weeks, as 
provided in §8(b) of the Act, for the Petitioner’s periods of disability from April 27, 2024 through 
May 5, 2024 and July 17, 2024 through August 19, 2024.   
 
 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that Respondent shall pay 
Petitioner permanent partial disability benefits of $751.18/ week for 43 weeks, as provided in §8(e) 
of the Act, because the injuries sustained caused the 20% loss of use of the right leg.   
 
 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that Petitioner is awarded 
reasonable and related medical outlined in PX1, pursuant to §8(a) and 8.2 of the Act.  
 
 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that Respondent shall have credit 
for all amounts paid, if any, to or on behalf of the Petitioner on account of said accidental injury. 
 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that Respondent shall receive 
credit for any bills paid by its group medical plan pursuant to §8(j).  Respondent shall hold 
Petitioner harmless for any bills for which they are claiming said credit.  
 
 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED BY THE COMMISSION that the Respondent pay to 
Petitioner interest under §19(n) of the Act, if any. 
 
Pursuant to §19(f)(1) of the Act, claims against the State of Illinois are not subject to 
judicial review. Therefore, no appeal bond is set in this case.

An Application for Adjustment of Claim was filed in this matter, and a Notice of Hearing was mailed to each 
party.  The matter was heard by the Honorable Edward Lee, Arbitrator of the Commission, in the city of 
Herrin, on June 3, 2025.  After reviewing all of the evidence presented, the Arbitrator hereby makes findings 
on the disputed issues checked below and attaches those findings to this document.  
DISPUTED ISSUES 
A. 
 Was Respondent operating under and subject to the Illinois Workers' Compensation or Occupational  
Diseases Act? 
B. 
 Was there an employee-employer relationship? 
C. 
 Did an accident occur that arose out of and in the course of Petitioner's employment by Respondent? 
D. 
 What was the date of the accident? 
E. 
 Was timely notice of the accident given to Respondent? 
F.

G.

H.

I. 
 What was Petitioner's marital status at the time of the accident? 
J.

 paid all appropriate charges for all reasonable and necessary medical services? 
K.

FINDINGS 
 
On April 26, 2024, Respondent was operating under and subject to the provisions of the Act.   
 
On this date, an employee-employer relationship did exist between Petitioner and Respondent.   
 
On this date, Petitioner did sustain an accident that arose out of and in the course of employment. 
 
Timely notice of this accident was given to Respondent. 
 
Petitioner's current condition of ill-being is causally related to the accident. 
 
In the year preceding the injury, Petitioner earned $65,102.66; the average weekly wage was $1,251.97. 
 
On the date of accident, Petitioner was 25 years of age, married with 1 dependent child(ren). 
 
Petitioner has received all reasonable and necessary medical services.   
 
Respondent has not paid all appropriate charges for all reasonable and necessary medical services. 
 
Respondent shall be given a credit of - for TTD, $- for TPD, $- for maintenance, and - for other benefits, for a 
total credit of $0. 
 
Respondent is entitled to a credit of any benefits paid under Section 8(j) of the Act. 
 
ORDER 
 
Respondent shall pay the reasonable and necessary medical services of outlined in Petitioner’s group exhibit 
related to the treatment of the injury, as provided in § 8(a) of the Act.   
 
Respondent shall be given credit for medical benefits that have been paid through its group carrier, and 
Respondent shall hold Petitioner harmless from any claims by any providers of the services for which 
Respondent is receiving this credit, as provided in § 8(j) of the Act.  
 
Respondent shall pay Petitioner temporary total disability benefits of $834.64/week for 6 weeks, as 
provided in Section 8(b) of the Act, for Petitioner’s periods of disability from April 27, 2024, through May 5, 
2024, and July 17, 2024, through August 19, 2024. 
 
Respondent shall pay Petitioner permanent partial disability benefits of $751.18/week for 43 weeks, because the 
injuries sustained caused the 20% loss of the right leg, as provided in § 8(e) of the Act.   
 
 
RULES REGARDING APPEALS  Unless a party files a Petition for Review within 30 days after receipt of this decision, 
and perfects a review in accordance with the Act and Rules, then this decision shall be entered as the decision of 
the Commission.   
 
STATEMENT OF INTEREST RATE  If the Commission reviews this award, interest at the rate set forth on the Notice of 
Decision of Arbitrator shall accrue from the date listed below to the day before the date of payment; however, if 
an employee's appeal results in either no change or a decrease in this award, interest shall not accrue.

MEMORANDUM OF DECISION OF ARBITRATOR 
 
FINDINGS OF FACT 
Background 
 
Petitioner testified that he currently works at Pinckneyville Correctional Center. (T.7) At 
the time of the accident, Petitioner was a 25-year-old Impact Program corrections officer at 
Murphysboro Life Skills Re-Entry Center. (T.8-9) He filed an Application for Adjustment of Claim 
for serious and permanent injury to his right knee/leg that occurred on April 26, 2024, during 
“State-sponsored activity.” (AX2) Petitioner testified that this was a basketball tournament 
arranged by Respondent. (T.14-15) Petitioner testified that he was asked to play in a basketball 
tournament by administration and was doing so when his right knee popped. (T.15-16) He denied 
prior injury or symptoms in his right knee, and he denied new accidents or injury to his right knee 
after the incident. (T.23) Respondent disputes accident, causal connection, liability for medical and 
temporary benefits, and the nature and extent of the injury. (AX1) 
Testimony and Documentary Evidence 
Petitioner testified that the Impact Program is a special program that is designed to redirect 
young inmates and instill adequate discipline and structure through physical fitness and life skills 
education. (T.8-9; PX9) His job required not only performance of regular correctional security 
duties, but also service as a behavioral mentor and physical fitness instructor during daily health 
and wellness sessions. (T.9-11) He provided a copy of Respondent’s staff manual, which was 
entered as his Exhibit 9, that outlined his responsibilities as a fitness instructor for the program. 
(PX9) The manual highlights the following: 
26IWCC0129

Humerickhouse, Clay 24WC012632 
Page 2 of 10 
• 
The primary goal of the Impact Program is to help reduce recidivism throughout the State 
of Illinois by attempting to rehabilitate the participant population with a structured skill 
attainment style environment, including:  
o "Positive Replacement: Replace all negative ideas and thoughts with positive 
ones."  
o "Focus on Negativity: Emphasize that the most crucial part is replacing negative 
thoughts."  
o Encourage Positive Actions: 
1. Promote healthy competition among participants. 
2. Foster an environment where positive actions are recognized and rewarded. 
3. Encourage teamwork and community involvement. Id. at p.4. 
In order to achieve the above, staff are instructed to engage in fitness activities to lead by 
example in health and wellness activities:  
S.  
Health and Wellness Involvement 
 
      10. Staff Involvement in Health and Wellness: 
o Lead by example by participating in exercise and wellness activities. 
o Demonstrate to participants that the tasks are achievable and motivate them 
through participation. Id. at p.7.  
 
Since staff is required to participate in such activities, under "STAFF Leadership and Conduct 
Standards," Respondent states, “6. Physical Fitness: Staff are encouraged to maintain an acceptable 
level of physical fitness.” Id. at p.8. Respondent also provides a list of approved activities and 
exercises. Id. at p.19-20. 
 
Petitioner testified that on the day of the accident, he was asked to play in a basketball 
tournament by administration, because Respondent did not have enough individuals in custody to 
fill the teams. (T.15) He was on the clock and getting paid at the time. (T.15) Petitioner stated that 
while he was dribbling the ball in-game, his right knee popped, he felt immediate pain, and fell to 
the ground. (T. 15) Since he was unable to bear weight on his right knee, he was escorted away in 
a wheelchair. (T.16) Petitioner testified that this tournament was part of the health and wellness 
activities that Respondent arranges for the inmates at its facility. (T.22) 
 
On cross-examination, Petitioner testified that while there was no mandate to participate in 
basketball, Respondent always encouraged the Impact Program staff to participate in the wellness 
activities. (T.24) He testified that Respondent also supplied the equipment and facilities for the 
game to be played. (T.25) 
 
 
26IWCC0129

Humerickhouse, Clay 24WC012632 
Page 3 of 10 
Respondent’s Exhibits  
 
Respondent’s Exhibit 2 is a Notice of Injury completed by Petitioner which consistently 
documented that he was injured when he felt a pop and pain while participating in a basketball 
tournament held by Respondent. (RX2) Respondent’s Exhibit 1, the Form 45, and Respondent’s 
Exhibit 3, a Supervisor’s Report of Injury or Illness, also both report that Petitioner was injured 
while playing basketball. (RX1; RX3) Respondent’s Exhibit 4 is a waiver completed by Petitioner 
on April 5, 2023, prior to the date of injury on April 26, 2024, which states that Petitioner agrees 
that should he sustain any “non-job related injury while utilizing the gymnasium and/or facility 
equipment at Murphysboro LSRC,” he would “not hold Murphysboro LSRC or the Illinois 
Department of Corrections liable.” (RX4) 
Testimony of Angela Isaacs 
 
Ms. Isaacs testified that she is employed as Superintendent of the Impact Program. (T.29) 
She testified that there is no mandate requiring correctional officers to do any type of physical 
activity to stay in shape in their job. (T.29-30) She testified that the sports equipment at the facility 
is supplied by the inmate benefit fund, but IDOC employees are allowed to use the equipment 
along with the inmates. (T.31)  
 
Ms. Isaacs testified that Respondent eschewed its former paramilitary-style program for 
“holistic” health and wellness program that focused on creating healthy habits for mind and body 
so that upon release the inmates would “make better choices.” (T.31-32) She testified that the role 
of correctional officers is to set an example for the inmates, “motivate them to be better human 
beings,” and lead the health and wellness programs. (T.32-33) She acknowledged that some 
officers are more active than others in leading the exercise programs. (T.33) She testified that she 
was “not a fan of contact sports” and discourages it because “they’re all males and they get a little 
competitive,” which can lead to injury. (T.33, 36) She also stated that basketball is not officially a 
part of the impact program. (T.34) She testified that she was unaware of who in the administration 
program would have asked Petitioner to participate in a contact sport during the inmates’ free time, 
but she admitted that it was absolutely possible that someone else in a supervisory position asked 
him to so. (T.34-35, 38-39) 
 
On cross-examination, Ms. Isaacs testified that Petitioner was a good employee that set a 
positive example for inmates and correctional officers. (T.37) She agreed that he embodied the 
goals the Impact Program and took the program goals seriously at all times. (T.37) She agreed that 
Petitioner was promoting health and wellness on April 26, 2024. (T.37) She testified that she did 
not wish to discourage Petitioner from being hands-on, but she would discourage any contact 
activities. (T.38) Although it was her opinion that Petitioner should not have participated in 
basketball on that date, she acknowledged that Petitioner was not and will not be disciplined for 
his participation in the game. (T.39)  
 
26IWCC0129

Humerickhouse, Clay 24WC012632 
Page 4 of 10 
Medical Treatment 
 
Petitioner was seen in the emergency department on the date of injury and reported the 
history of his basketball injury and inability to put pressure on his right knee. (PX3) He reported 
that he was playing basketball when he “heard a pop and went down.” Id. He rated his pain as 4/10 
and had difficulty with extension. Id. Examination revealed painful and limited range of motion in 
the right knee with crepitus and swelling along the suprapatellar region indicative of early effusion. 
Id. X-rays were negative for fracture or dislocation. Id. He was given crutches and pain medication 
with instructions to use ice and analgesics, referred for an orthopedic evaluation, and advised to 
follow-up with his family physician as well. Id.  
 
Petitioner was seen at the Orthopaedic Institute of Southern Illinois on April 30, 2024, 
where the history of his injury and symptoms were again noted, and physical examination again 
revealed effusion as well as positive McMurray’s test and limited range of motion. (PX4) PA-C 
Palmer recommended an MRI scan, but was unable to get it approved, at which time Petitioner 
sought a second opinion with Dr. Matthew Bradley. (PX5)  
On May 9, 2024, Dr. Bradley evaluated Petitioner and noted that Petitioner injured his right 
knee on April 26, 2024, when his knee popped while playing basketball at work. (PX5) He noted 
that Petitioner had no prior history of injury or significant complaints in his right knee. Id. 
Although Petitioner’s swelling was better, it was still present, and he continued to have significant 
pain and difficulty extending his right knee. Id. Dr. Bradley’s examination was positive for pain 
with McMurray’s testing, crepitus, and difficulty extending his knee, which Dr. Bradley noted was 
consistent with his findings on x-ray. Id. He also causally related Petitioner’s current complaints 
to the work accident and sent Petitioner for an MRI. Id.  
An MRI was obtained later that day and showed a bucket-handle-type tear of the medial 
meniscus with an associated large displaced meniscal fragment into the interior portion of the 
medial tibiofemoral compartment, a full-thickness ACL tear, bone contusions in the lateral tibial 
and medial femoral condyles, focal Grade-IV chondral fissure in the medial patellar articulation, 
and hemarthrosis. (PX6) Petitioner returned to Dr. Bradley on May 20, 2024, with ongoing 
instability and severe knee pain. (PX5) Dr. Bradley reviewed the findings and recommended 
surgery. Id. 
On July 17, 2024, Dr. Bradley performed arthroscopic anterior crucial ligament 
reconstruction, excision of a large bucket handle medial meniscus tear, and chondroplasty of the 
medial femoral condyle. Id.; (PX7) Objective intraoperative findings confirmed a complete rupture 
of the anterior cruciate ligament from the femoral attachment and a very large bucket handle, 
white-white medial meniscus tear that was flipped into the intercondylar notch from the posterior 
root all the way around to the anterior root involving approximately 50% to 60% of the medial 
meniscus involved. Id. Petitioner did well following surgery and returned to Dr. Bradley on August 
1, 2024, and reported marked improvement in pain. (PX5) Dr. Bradley believed Petitioner was 
well enough to start rehabilitation and prescribed physical therapy. Id.  
26IWCC0129

Humerickhouse, Clay 24WC012632 
Page 5 of 10 
  
 Petitioner began therapy at SIH Outpatient Rehab and then returned to Dr. Bradley on 
September 26, 2024. (PX5) He reported that he continued to do well and was making excellent 
progress, so Dr. Bradley believed Petitioner was ready to return to full-duty work. Id. Dr. Bradley 
advised, however, that Petitioner should continue to do physical therapy and refrain from 
performing any kind of twisting, turning, strenuous activity. Id.  
 
On December 3, 2024, Petitioner continued to do extremely well and was working full duty 
without incident. Id. Dr. Bradley believed Petitioner reached maximum medical improvement, but 
he continued to recommend that Petitioner continue his home exercise program to promote 
strength and flexibility of his knee. Id.  
 
Petitioner testified that despite the improvement from treatment, he still has reduced range 
of motion and residual symptoms that increase with activity. (T.20) He stated that he has persistent 
right knee popping, and his knee gets fatigued easily with use. (T.20) He hopes to improve his 
strength and endurance by continuing his home exercise program. (T.20) He also is hesitant to 
engage in substantial activity both in and outside of work out of fear of reinjury. (T.21-22) 
 
Respondent did not have Petitioner examined.  
 
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW 
Issue (C): 
Did an accident occur that arose out of and in the course of Petitioner’s 
employment by Respondent? 
 
“Compensation may be allowed where the employee's existing physical structure, 
whatever it may be, gives way under the stress of his usual labor and he is suddenly disabled. This 
is true even though the result would not have obtained had he been in normal health.”  Int'l 
Harvester Co. v. Indus. Comm'n, 56 Ill. 2d 84, 90, 305 N.E.2d 529, 533 (1973). Said labor, 
however, must “arise out of” and “in the course of” employment. 820 ILCS 305/1(d). 
“The ‘arising out of’ component is primarily concerned with causal connection. To satisfy 
this requirement it must be shown that the injury had its origin in some risk connected with, or 
incidental to, the employment to create a causal connection between the employment and the 
accidental injury.” McAllister v. Illinois Workers' Comp. Comm'n, 2020 IL 124848, 181 N.E.3d 
656, citing Sisbro, 207 Ill. 2d 193 at 203 (citing Caterpillar Tractor, 129 Ill.2d 52); see also 
Baggett v. Industrial Comm’n, 201 Ill. 2d 187, 194 (2002) (“An injury ‘arises out of’ one’s 
employment if it originates from a risk connected with, or incidental to, the employment, involving 
a causal connection between the employment and the accidental injury.”). A risk is incidental to 
the employment when it belongs to or relates to what the employee must do in fulfilling his or her 
job duties. McAllister, citing Orsini, 117 Ill. 2d at 45. A risk is distinctly associated with an 
employee’s employment if, at the time of the occurrence, the employee was performing (1) acts 
he or she was instructed to perform by the employer, (2) acts that he or she had a common-law or 
statutory duty to perform, or (3) acts that the employee might reasonably be expected to perform 
26IWCC0129

Humerickhouse, Clay 24WC012632 
Page 6 of 10 
incident to his or her assigned duties. McAllister, citing Caterpillar Tractor, 129 Ill. 2d at 58; see 
also The Venture—Newberg-Perini, Stone & Webster v. Illinois Workers’ Compensation Comm’n, 
2013 IL 115728, ¶ 18; Sisbro, 207 Ill. 2d 193 at 204. 
Petitioner’s testimony that he was performing an activity he was instructed to perform is 
unrebutted and satisfies the prima facie requirements of the Act regarding accident. Respondent, 
however, maintains that no compensable accident occurred. Respondent asserts that 1) the claim 
is barred by Section 11 of the Act, that 2) Petitioner’s activity was unauthorized by Respondent, 
and 3) that Petitioner waived his right to recovery.  
With regard to whether Petitioner’s claim is barred by Section 11 of the Act, the Arbitrator 
finds that precedent does not support that Petitioner’s activity fell within the meaning of voluntary 
recreational activity under the Act. As courts have often noted, the plain and ordinary meaning of 
“recreation” according to Webster’s Dictionary is “the act of recreating or the state of being 
recreated: refreshment of the strength and spirits after toil: DIVERSON, PLAY.” Elmhurst Park 
Dist. v. Illinois Workers' Comp. Comm'n, 395 Ill. App. 3d 404, 409, 917 N.E.2d 1052, 1057 (2009). 
This may include “stopping work, sharing common food and drink, socializing,” or similar 
activities. Helping Hands Ctr. v. Illinois Workers' Comp. Comm'n, 2024 IL App (1st) 240057WC-
U, ¶ 17. However, courts recognize that under some circumstances, an activity that would 
ordinarily be considered “recreation” may in fact be a work-related activity. 
In Elmhurst Park Dist. v. Illinois Workers’ Comp. Comm’n, the Court held that even a 
"recreational activity" may be compensable where “recreation” is inherent in the claimant's 
position. Elmhurst Park Dist. v. Illinois Workers' Comp. Comm'n, 395 Ill. App. 3d 404, 917 N.E.2d 
1052 (2009). In that case, the claimant was a fitness instructor for his employer who was injured 
while participating in a “wallyball” game held by his employer at a coworker’s request. Id. The 
claimant initially declined a coworker’s (McElroy's) invitation to participate in the wallyball game, 
but after McElroy’s persistence and being told the game didn’t have enough players and would be 
cancelled without his participation, the claimant decided to assist because he “felt that [it] was part 
of [his] job” to promote different classes and programs. Id. Based on that evidence, the Court 
determined that the claimant did not participate in the wallyball game for his own “diversion” or 
to “refresh” or “strengthen” his spirits after toil, but he did so to accommodate respondent's 
customers. Id. It held: 
[W]e can certainly envision circumstances under which participation in a game of 
wallyball would constitute a “recreational” activity and therefore fall within the 
voluntary-recreational activity exclusion set forth in section 11 of the Act. 
However, we do not believe that the facts of this case present such a situation . . . 
[Here] [C]laimant decided to “help[ ] out” because he “felt that [it] was part of [his] 
job” which was “to promote * * * different classes and programs.” Based on this 
evidence, we conclude that claimant did not participate in the wallyball game for 
his own “diversion” or to “refresh” or “strengthen” his spirits after toil. Rather, 
26IWCC0129

Humerickhouse, Clay 24WC012632 
Page 7 of 10 
claimant participated in the game to accommodate respondent's customers. As such, 
we find that claimant was not engaged in a “recreational” activity as contemplated 
by section 11 of the Act at the time of his injury. Elmhurst Park Dist. v. Illinois 
Workers' Comp. Comm'n, 395 Ill. App. 3d 404, 409, 917 N.E.2d 1052, 1057 (2009). 
 
Similarly, in Calumet, the claimant was a middle school teacher who was asked to 
participate in an after-school basketball game by the school principal. Calumet School Dist. No. 
132 v. Illinois Workers Comp. Comm’n, 2016 IL App (1st) 153034WC, 67 N.E.3d 966. Claimant 
was not a basketball player and did not wish to participate but did so since attendance and 
participation in after-school events involving students was part of claimant’s job. Id. Consequently, 
the Court found that the evidence was sufficient to support the determination that the claimant was 
not involved in a voluntary recreational program. Id.  
 
Much like the above cases, Petitioner in this case, along with a fellow employee, were 
asked by a supervisor to participate in a basketball tournament because there were not enough 
players in the game. (T.14-15, 38-39)  In addition, it is undisputed that being a health and wellness 
instructor was part of his job duties. (PX9) Respondent’s own employee handbook instructs 
employees to “[l]ead by example by participating in exercise and wellness activities.” Id. at p.7. 
The program guidelines also encourage “healthy competition” among inmates. Id. at 4. As 
Petitioner was performing an activity within the scope of his employment as requested by senior 
staff, the Arbitrator finds that Petitioner was not engaged in a recreational activity precluded by 
Section 11 of the Act at the time of accident.  
 
Although Respondent’s asserts that Petitioner’s claim should be denied since basketball 
was allegedly prohibited by Respondent’s rules, the Arbitrator concludes that under the 
circumstances this is no bar to compensation. In this case, Petitioner was not engaging in an activity 
of his own volition to voluntarily endanger himself, but he participated in an event arranged by 
Respondent at the request of his supervisor. (T.14-15) While Ms. Isaacs did not believe that such 
activities should be held, it is clear that others in supervisory capacities did not agree. Moreover, 
Ms. Isaacs confirmed that Petitioner was not and will not be disciplined for his actions. (T.39) The 
Arbitrator does not find it reasonable to penalize an employee who was following orders from a 
superior officer in performance of an activity to further the interests and goals of Respondent. The 
Arbitrator notes that there is also support in precedent for allowing compensation in cases where 
injury occurs during an activity that is technically prohibited by an employer but is still generally 
allowed in common practice.  
In David Moore v. Brookwood School District, the Commission noted that two of the 
claimant’s co-workers, and fellow custodians, testified that the custodian had been instructed not 
to move any heavy furniture such as cabinets or bookshelves. David Moore v. Brookwood School 
District, 11 IL. W.C. 39031 (Ill. Indus. Comm'n Jan. 28, 2016). Yet, the Commission noted, a 
dolly was made available to the custodians for moving items. When questioned about the dolly, 
the claimant’s supervisor, testified that it was used to move items that could not be carried.

In Harris, IV (Minor) v. City of Mascoutah, the claimant was a lifeguard who was injured 
on break when he performed a back dive into Respondent’s pool. Harris IV (Minor) by Harris III 
(Father) v. City of Mascoutah, 22 I.W.C.C. 0385, aff’d by 2024 IL App (5th) 230480WC-U. 
Although there was a rule prohibiting back dives, the claimant was unaware of same and was 
imitating senior staff when he performed a back dive into the pool after another employee. Id. In 
addition, the active lifeguard did not blow the whistle indicating a rule violation in any of the 
instances where the back dive was performed. Id. The Commission thus affirmed that the claimant 
did not leave the course and scope of his employment in performing the activity, as Petitioner was 
engaged in a compensable act of personal comfort that was incidental to employment and did not 
perform the activity in an unreasonable manner. Id.  
Here, Petitioner was performing an act incidental to his employment. He was fulfilling the 
request of a supervisor to engage in an activity that was arranged by Respondent. Respondent also 
provided the equipment. The Arbitrator therefore finds that Petitioner was still acting within the 
course and scope of his employment at the time of his accident.   
 
Finally, the Arbitrator notes that Respondent’s Exhibit 4 is entirely irrelevant to the matter 
at hand. There is no foundation or context as to the reason for this form. As noted above, Petitioner 
was engaged in a work-related activity; the form purports to preclude liability for “non-job related” 
injuries. (RX4) The law and public policy bars Respondent from seeking to compel waiver of 
workers’ compensation rights without the approval of the Commission. Section 23 states, “No 
employee, personal representative, or beneficiary shall have power to waive any of the provisions 
of this Act” without prior approval by the Commission. 820 ILCS 305/23. Even if the parties had 
intended to waive the right to such litigation, any agreement contrary to law and the public policy 
of this State is null and void. Id.; P.I. & I. Motor Exp., Inc./For U, LLC v. Indus. Comm'n, 368 Ill. 
App. 3d 230, 857 N.E.2d 784 (2006) (Any agreement between an employer and an employee 
which purports to divest the Workers' Compensation Commission of jurisdiction where it 
otherwise exists is contrary to the public policy of the State and is, therefore, unenforceable.) 
 
Based upon the foregoing, the Arbitrator finds that Petitioner satisfied his burden in 
proving that he suffered accidental injuries that arose out of and in the course of his employment 
with Respondent.

Issue (J): 
Were the medical services that were provided to Petitioner reasonable and 
necessary? Has Respondent paid all appropriate charges for all reasonable and 
necessary medical services? 
 
Upon establishing causal connection and the reasonableness and necessity of 
recommended medical treatment, employers are responsible for necessary medical care required 
by their employees. Plantation Mfg. Co. v. Indus. Comm’n, 294 Ill.App.3d 705, 691 N.E.2d 13 
(Ill. 2000). This includes treatment required to diagnose, relieve, or cure the effects of claimant's 
injury.  F & B Mfg. Co. v. Indus. Comm'n, 325 Ill.App.3d 527, 758 N.E.2d 18 (1st Dist. 2001). 
Petitioner’s objective MRI studies and objective intraoperative findings showed substantial 
injury with a large bucket-handle-type tear of the medial meniscus and a full-thickness ACL tear 
with bone contusions. (PX5; PX6) The severity of the pathology required extensive surgical repair, 
which improved Petitioner’s condition significantly.  
Respondent is therefore ordered to pay the medical bills contained in Petitioner’s group 
exhibit. Respondent shall have credit for expenses which have been paid through its group health 
coverage, but it shall indemnify and hold Petitioner harmless from any claims arising out of the 
expenses for which it claims credit.

Issue (L): 
What is the nature and extent of the injury? 
  
Pursuant to § 8.1b of the Act, permanent partial disability from injuries that occur after 
September 1, 2011, are to be established using the following criteria: (i) the reported level of 
impairment pursuant to subsection (a) of the Act; (ii) the occupation of the injured employee; (iii) 
the age of the employee at the time of the injury; (iv) the employee’s future earning capacity; and 
(v) evidence of disability corroborated by the treating medical records. 820 ILCS 305/8.1b. The 
Act provides that, “No single enumerated factor shall be the sole determinant of disability.” 820 
ILCS 305/8.1b(b)(v). 
i.Level of Impairment: Neither party submitted an AMA rating. Therefore, the Arbitrator 
places no weight on this factor.  
ii.Occupation:  Petitioner is still employed as a Correctional Officer but works at its 
Pinckneyville facility. (T.7) The Arbitrator places greater weight on this factor. 
iii.Age:  Petitioner was 25 years old at the time of his injury. He is very young and must live 
with his concerns for most of his work life expectancy. The Arbitrator places some weight 
on this factor.  
iv.Earning Capacity: There is no evidence of reduced earning capacity. The Arbitrator 
assigns lesser weight to this factor. 
v.Disability: As a result of his accident, Petitioner suffered substantial right knee injuries, 
including bone contusions and tears to his meniscus and ACL, which required arthroscopic 
anterior crucial ligament reconstruction, excision of a large bucket handle medial meniscus 
tear, and chondroplasty of the medial femoral condyle. (PX5; PX7) Petitioner testified that 
despite the improvement from treatment, he still has reduced range of motion and residual 
symptoms that increase with activity. (T.20) He stated that he has persistent right knee 
popping, and his knee gets fatigued easily with use. (T.20) He hopes to improve his strength 
and endurance by continuing his home exercise program. (T.20) He also is hesitant to 
engage in substantial activity both in and outside of work out of fear of reinjury. (T.21-22) 
The Arbitrator finds his complaints proportionate with his injury sustained and generally 
supported by the records.  
Based upon the foregoing, the Arbitrator finds that Petitioner suffered the 20% loss of his right 
leg.
